en: She kept as her own child.
Reunited with Kanykei,
When Kumaiyk stood weeping,
The birch wept, the willow wept;
Every soul watching wept.
The white-bearded old man wept;
The people wept, the multitude wept.
All populous Bukhara wept;
Those who held themselves great wept;
Her father Temir Khan wept.
Ysmayyl of Bukhara,
Temir Khan and Koloi Khan,
With Shaatemir, those four,
Had six matching gray mares
Slaughtered in sacrifice,
Quickly pledging an offering to Bahauddin.
All populous Bukhara sobbed,
Crying out, “My orphan!”
Had he not raised him?
Ysmayyl wept on one side.
“My one and only morning star—
Who knows his worth?
If the boy goes about like this,
Someone's evil eye will strike him,” he said.
Raised at the treasury's expense,
Nine black bulls
He had driven to him;
As a votive offering, all of them
He had beheaded.
The khoja in a motley robe,
The mullah in a white turban,
Those nine black bulls
He had them cut apart.
Performing a rite for the boy,
He had them slaughtered as an offering.
Leaving no rite unperformed,
Unwilling to accept their rites,
Semetey, whom you have seen,
Would not turn his heart toward Bukhara.
Truly created by God,
Did you see that he was His servant?
Poor Manas the warrior—
Did you see that he was his son?
His father's son,
As his descendant after him,
Has remained—do you see?"
Then the boy said:
"I have found a land like broad Talas.
I have found a people granted by fate.
I have found a people full of joy;
I have found a land ordained by fortune.
Until I go to my people, my kinsfolk,
I shall never turn aside.
Until I reach my people, I shall not rest."
Turning toward Kanykei,
These were the words he spoke:
"Should a nobleman's only son
Have cause to wander in exile?
Unfortunate mother, where are my people?
Should the son of a prince
Have cause to flee?
Wretched mother, where are my people?
Fleeing from my people,
You came and settled in Bukhara.
You had them call you a fugitive woman;
You earned a bad name.
Acting with great folly,
Wandering away from my people,
You reached Bukhara and settled.
You had them call you a wayward woman;
You earned a bad name.
Fleeing to your birth family,
Shameless mother, you settled comfortably.
The offspring of a noble line
You had them call a wandering orphan.
You gave me a bad name.
Coming to your birth family and thriving,
You, a lord's wife, settled comfortably.
The son of a prince
You had your younger brother Ysmayyl raise.
Such a spectacle you have made!
When you fled here from Bukhara,
When you scattered your wealth,
Riding Taitoru as your mount,
You brought me to Bukhara,
Making me a stranger to my kin.
The descendant of a populous land—
Why should I live exiled from my people?
Now, Bukhara, farewell!
Let me go toward my people.
I shall move away openly, people of Bukhara.
I am going to Talas.
If there is an enemy who fights me,
I shall put an end to them all.
If a mighty host bears me enmity,
My wrath will rise and I shall stand firm.
I shall put an end to them all!
This year I shall move to Talas.
Sarytaz, who burns charcoal,
I shall take to Talas,
Raise him as khan of the Argyn,
And make him a sultan.
Sary Khan is no ordinary man.
I have named him Sary Khan.
You many people of the city of Bukhara,
You, the khan, stand here.
This elder Sary of mine,
Blackened with soot from burning charcoal,
Was master of Kul-Tokoi.
People of Bukhara, when did you heed God?
Making him a slave to burn charcoal,
You beat my elder Sary.
The name Sarytaz has vanished.
Now he has prospered as Sary Khan.
Growing to maturity as an orphan,
My elder has joined the ranks.
His humiliation was scattered into the forest.
My elder Sary's eyes have opened wide.
Without quarreling, people of Bukhara,
Give me my elder Sary.
Clothe him in a coat no bullet can pierce;
Mount him on a horse no bullet can catch.
Bakai and Sary Khan,
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
Abyke and Chynkozho—
These are my named kinsmen.
If I do not bind them to my side,
From Kongurbai in Beijing,
If I do not avenge my father Manas's death!
Against the teeming unbelievers
The time has come to open a holy war.
Upon the hero Khan Kongurbai,
Upon the land of Machanchyn,
Upon the people of Chynmachyn,
I shall truly bring slaughter.
My true father's mighty vengeance
I shall exact from Kakanchyn.
My aged elder Bakai
I shall have lead the way.
Sarytaz, with eyes like cups,
I shall have carry the banner.
Across Altai and Kakanchyn,
I shall raid without leaving a place untouched.
Upon the Chinese, numerous as ants,
I shall bring fierce battle.
Upon the Black Kalmyks and the Shibee,
I shall wreak havoc.
All the vengeance owed my father,
I shall exact from the unbelievers!
Not only the Chinese, people of Bukhara,
Many lands have their eyes upon me.
I have many enemies to battle.
Do not oppose me, people of Bukhara.
I shall move to Talas.
I shall arrive and settle close
To my departed father Manas.
I will not forget, people of Bukhara,
This trouble you have caused.
Until I reached twelve years of age,
You made me call my mother my elder sister,
And concealed my father from me.
Your father's grave, people of Bukhara!
Now I have found my father—shall I lie idle?
If you strut about, people of Bukhara,
I shall seize your goods by force.
If you swagger about, people of Bukhara,
I shall exact even greater redress."
When the boy spoke thus,
All the people of Bukhara,
Khan Temir and Ysmayyl,
Koloy and Shaatemir,
The people all gathered.
Temir Khan, khan of Bukhara,
With tears flowing down his beard,
With tears pouring from his eyes,
His heart deeply troubled,
Hung his belt about his neck,
And pleaded with Semetey:
"My darling Semetey!
My lamp on whom I lean,
You have set out toward your people.
Let Bukhara lie empty!
Thus you have left it desolate.
My darling foal!
When you leave Bukhara,
When you reach your own people,
When you go and settle in Talas,
When you are truly Kyrgyz,
This desolate Bukhara
You have left impoverished.
Your whip with a hawthorn handle—
Who will fit it without twisting it?
When you go to Talas,
This wretched people of Bukhara—
Who will lead them without scattering them?
The dark-bladed battle-axe—
Who will fit it without tilting it?
Desolate Bukhara—
Who will lead it as its support?
When you came to Bukhara an orphan,
I had ninety animals slaughtered for your feast.
I had them call you Ysmayyl's son;
I had your ancestry altered.
I thought of what might come to pass.
When you came to Bukhara,
I held a feast for eighty days.
Lest someone's evil eye strike you,
I had prayers recited and an amulet fastened at your neck.
In summer's hot days,
Lest the heat strike you,
I had you reared in the shade.
So your heart would grow fat,
I had unbred mares slaughtered,
Had finely chopped boiled meat served,
And fed you your fill of rib fat.
So you would become a surpassing hero,
I had hunters gathered,
Sent them on a hunting expedition,
Had them shoot and bring back a tiger,
And had its heart given to you.
Until you reached twelve years of age,
To the court where you stayed
I had wrestlers gathered.
Of the people who came unaware,
I had quite a few killed.
When you were six years old,
I entrusted you to a mullah,
And had you taught to be a scholar.
So you would become a marksman,
When you reached twelve years of age,
I had you shoot wild game on the plain.
So you would grow skilled,
I taught you the ways of war.
'If my son stays in Bukhara,
When I rise early tomorrow,
I shall slice and eat horse rump,' I thought.
'If a dark enemy opposes us,
I shall crush the Chinese governor,' I thought.
'If my son stays in Bukhara,
With a pine-shafted spear and keen steel,
I shall pierce through,' I thought.
'Against an enemy who opposes us,
I shall press my attack,' I thought.
Since your people are different,
You have set out toward the Kyrgyz.
Bukhara, red gold,
You have left desolate here.
When you leave Bukhara,
If the dark moon is clouded over,
What shall we do with the night?
'The boy has left Bukhara,' they will say.
If enemies besiege and attack us,
What shall we do with the day?
My precious son, hear my words.
On my right are the Russians;
On my left are the Six Cities and Kokand.
